client: I've been feeling really off ever since my breakup with Maria about three months ago. Like, things I used to love doing, hiking with friends for example, just don't bring me any joy anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and reaching out — it takes real courage to try something even when part of you isn't sure it will help, and I want you to know that ambivalence is completely normal. What you're describing, losing interest in things that used to bring you joy like hiking, is something we can absolutely work through together. I'm curious — when you think about those moments with friends on the trail now, what tends to go through your mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I picture being out there with them, the first thing that hits me is this wave of guilt — like I don't deserve to enjoy myself when I've been such a flaky friend lately. I keep canceling plans and then telling myself I'll make it up to them, but I never really do, and I think part of me is afraid they're just... tired of waiting for me to show up. It's easier to stay home than to face that, I guess.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — feeling like you don't deserve joy and that your friends might be giving up on you — sounds really heavy to carry, and it makes so much sense that staying home feels safer than risking that fear. I'm noticing something worth gently exploring though: that thought "I don't deserve to enjoy myself" sounds like a pretty harsh judgment you're making about yourself — I'm wondering, is that something you'd say to a friend who was struggling the way you are right now? What do you think is driving that belief that you've somehow forfeited your right to feel good?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: No, I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably tell them they deserve to feel happy, that struggling doesn't mean you've done something wrong. But it feels different when it's me, like there's a separate set of rules that apply to my situation specifically. I think part of what's driving it is this feeling that I've been pulling away from people for months and letting friendships fade, and that feels like something I actually did wrong, not just something that happened to me.
therapist: You've just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you would someone you care about, and that's such a common but painful double standard that we can really work with. It sounds like underneath the guilt is an actual fear that your actions during a really hard time have caused real damage to your friendships, and that feels more concrete and scary than just "struggling." I'm wondering — when you imagine reaching out to one of those friends today, what's the story you tell yourself about how they'd actually respond?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, when I imagine reaching out, the first thing that comes to mind is that they'd be polite but distant, like they'd respond out of obligation rather than actually wanting to hear from me. I keep thinking they've probably moved on and built their lives without me in them, and reaching out would just remind them of how unreliable I was when things got hard. It's like I've already decided the outcome before anything even happens, and I know that sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it feels completely true in my gut.
therapist: You've actually named something really significant yourself — that you've already decided the outcome before anything happens, which in CBT we'd call a kind of "mind reading," and it's striking how clearly you can see it intellectually even while it feels completely real emotionally. That gap between knowing something sounds irrational and still feeling it as absolute truth is actually one of the most important things we can work with together. I'm curious — can you think of any small piece of evidence, even one, that might not fit the story that your friends have fully moved on and are just waiting politely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... there is this one thing that keeps nagging at me. My friend Priya texted me last week just to send me a meme she thought I'd find funny — not because we had plans or anything, just out of nowhere. But then my brain immediately went to "she's just being nice, she feels obligated," so I kind of dismissed it, which I guess is exactly what you're talking about.
therapist: You just caught your own mind doing exactly that thing in real time — taking a genuinely warm gesture from Priya and immediately reframing it as obligation, which is a really important thing to notice. The fact that she reached out with something playful and personal, not just a "how are you" check-in, actually sounds like someone who was thinking of you just because you crossed her mind. What do you think it would mean for you — about yourself, about the friendship — if you let yourself take that gesture at face value, just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... if I actually let myself believe she was just thinking of me, that feels kind of nice for a second, but then it almost immediately feels scary. Like, what if I start counting on that, and then she disappears again the way people do? I think part of me keeps it at arm's length on purpose, because hoping feels more dangerous than just assuming it doesn't mean much.
therapist: What you just described — keeping hope at arm's length to protect yourself from being hurt — is such a deeply human response, and the way you said it, softly and carefully, makes me think this fear of being left runs really deep for you. It sounds like somewhere along the way you learned that hoping for connection is more dangerous than the loneliness of not hoping, which is a really painful place to live. I'm wondering — do you have a sense of where that belief first took root, or does it feel connected to what happened with Maria, or maybe something even older than that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it goes back further than Maria, honestly. There was a lot of growing up where I felt like I was kind of invisible to the people who were supposed to see me most, and I learned pretty early that wanting too much from people just set you up for disappointment. Maria just... confirmed what I already suspected was true about me and connection.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — that this isn't a new wound Maria created, but an old one she reopened, this sense of being invisible to the people who mattered most and learning to want less to stay safe. There's something quietly heartbreaking about a younger version of you deciding that needing people was the problem, rather than the people who weren't showing up for you. I want to sit with that for a moment — when you say Maria "confirmed what you already suspected about yourself," what is it exactly that you believe she confirmed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That I'm just... too much to deal with, but also somehow not enough at the same time. Like, I take up space in a way that exhausts people, but I'm also not interesting or worthwhile enough for them to actually stay. When Maria pulled away without really explaining why, it felt like proof of something I'd been carrying around for years — that if people really get to know me, they eventually decide I'm not worth the effort.
therapist: That belief — "too much and not enough at the same time" — is one of the most painful contradictions a person can carry, and I can hear how long and how quietly you've been holding that. What strikes me is that Maria's silence became evidence for a verdict you'd already been afraid was true, but silence isn't actually an explanation — it's just an absence, and we often fill absences with our deepest fears about ourselves. I want to gently ask — is it possible that what felt like proof was actually just a story you reached for because it was familiar, not because it was true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it's just a story I made up. But it doesn't feel like I just reached for it out of nowhere — it feels like every time I've gotten close to someone, eventually they pull away, and that pattern has to mean something about me. It's hard to call it just a fear when it keeps happening over and over.
therapist: The pain in what you're saying is real, and I don't want to dismiss the pattern you've experienced — those losses are genuine, and it makes complete sense that your mind is trying to find a reason for them. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: a pattern of people pulling away could say something about the kinds of connections you've sought out, or the walls you've built to stay safe, rather than something fundamentally wrong with who you are. I'm wondering — in those relationships where people eventually pulled away, were there ever moments early on where something felt a little off, or where you found yourself shrinking to make them more comfortable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, there probably were moments like that, but I don't know if I can trust my own memory on this stuff anymore. Like, I think I do shrink a lot — I catch myself agreeing with things I don't actually agree with, or laughing off things that actually bothered me. But honestly, that just makes me feel worse, because now it sounds like you're saying it's kind of my fault they left.
therapist: Oh, I want to stop right there — that is not at all what I meant, and I'm really glad you named that because the last thing I want is for this to become another reason to be hard on yourself. Shrinking yourself around people isn't a flaw or a cause of abandonment — it's actually a really understandable strategy you developed to stay safe, probably going all the way back to those early experiences of feeling invisible. The question I'm more interested in is what it might feel like to slowly, carefully, start taking up a little more of your own space — not as something you failed to do before, but as something that might be possible now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
